SMTO-HTTP-0067 — This request has too many headers

GUID: a0822dff-1a2d-4b7c-b172-d06a9288fa7e
Slug: http-header-limit
Domain: HTTP · Subsystem: http

What happened

  • Web requests can carry at most 64 extra labeled details, called headers, adding up to about 32 KB, including the sign-in details SMTO adds. This request went over that limit, or its headers weren't a simple list, so it wasn't sent.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Ask the Agent to resend the request with only the headers the service's documentation requires. Fewer headers keep the request under SMTO's size limit.
  2. If the request uses a saved connection, open it in Parameter Store and remove unneeded entries under Default header in Advanced connection settings, then select Save. Default headers are added to every request, so extra ones use up the limit each time.
  3. Keep the sign-in header the service requires and trim other headers instead. Without its sign-in header, the service would refuse the request.

What success looks like

  • The Agent's request is sent and returns a result from the service.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages SMTO. Don't remove sign-in details or saved data to get under the limit.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • Header validation rejected the headers: they are not an object, there are more than 64 entries, or their combined size exceeds 32 KiB including profile default headers and runtime authentication.

What this means

  • Header input is not an object, contains over 64 entries, or encoded/assembled header size exceeds 32 KiB including runtime authentication. The specific receipt owns dispatch and effect truth. Authentication exchanges, resource requests and Gateway admission are separate phases; rendering this explanation performs no request and never authorizes replay of an uncertain mutation.

Why this can happen

  • Header input is not an object, contains over 64 entries, or encoded/assembled header size exceeds 32 KiB including runtime authentication.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect header count, object shape and aggregate encoded bytes including injected authentication.

How to fix it

  • Pass headers as a name-to-value object with at most 64 entries and under 32 KiB combined, counting the profile's default_headers and injected authentication headers. Drop unnecessary or very large headers while keeping required authentication.
  • Use a header object within the 64-entry and 32 KiB bounds, retaining valid required authentication.

Retry and execution caution

  • Correct the recorded cause, then inspect current state and existing receipts before requesting another attempt.

How to verify the fix

  • The supported header object fits both count and byte bounds without truncating required values.

What not to do

  • Do not erase authoritative receipts or protected current input to conceal a size/capacity problem.

Technical notes

  • The specific receipt owns dispatch and effect truth. Authentication exchanges, resource requests and Gateway admission are separate phases; rendering this explanation performs no request and never authorizes replay of an uncertain mutation.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
